unit_label: Module C unit 3 (courseware unit 19), part 1: working capital concept, operating cycle, assessment methods, bills finance mechanics, letter of credit limit assessment

facts.statement: Most business enterprises, besides fixed assets, must carry current assets such as raw materials, work in process, finished goods and receivables; the money blocked in these current assets is working capital. The total requirement of current assets of an enterprise is the total or gross working capital. It is met partly by short-term credit available (including bank finance and credit from suppliers) and partly by funds the enterprise arranges from long-term sources (capital or long-term borrowings), which is called Net Working Capital (NWC). Working capital finance by the banks is the assessment of total current assets needed and how this need is to be met; the bank asks the enterprise to bring in part of the requirement from its own capital or long-term borrowings.

The normal operations of a business consist of purchase of raw materials, conversion into finished goods, sale on cash or credit, receipt of cash and purchase of raw materials again; this is the working capital cycle or operating cycle. Its length depends on the stocks of raw materials to be held, the time the process takes to convert raw materials into finished goods (work in process), the stock of finished goods carried before sale and the credit provided to purchasers. The longer the cycle, the larger the working capital requirement; correct assessment of the cycle is the most important part of the bank's assessment of gross working capital, net working capital and the bank finance.

For a banker the liquidity ratios, especially the current ratio, are important in assessment, sanctioning and monitoring. The assessment involves stipulating a minimum NWC that the enterprise must bring in from long-term sources, which results in a minimum current ratio (more than one) that the bank wants the enterprise to maintain at all times; it is normally part of the terms and conditions of the sanction and a tool for the bank to monitor the use of funds.

The holding norms based method, also called the operating cycle method or traditional method, first decides the level of turnover (for existing enterprises on past performance; for new enterprises on production capacity, proposed market share, availability of raw materials and industry norms). It then assesses gross working capital as the sum of its components: inventory (raw materials, work in process and finished goods, using lead time, minimum order quantity, location and number of suppliers, percentage of imported material and manufacturing process; banks can now estimate levels in each case and industry norms are used as a guide); receivables or bills (governed by market practice); and other current assets such as cash, advances to suppliers and advance tax. The sources for meeting the requirement are own sources (NWC from the last balance sheet plus internal accruals, with additional NWC stipulated if needed for the desired current ratio), suppliers' credit, other current liabilities (salaries and other expenses payable, advances from customers) and bank finance. Logically, bank finance equals the gap between total working capital and the funds available from all the other sources.

The recommendations of the Tandon committee gave three methods of lending, still found in some banks' calculations. In the first method the enterprise brings in NWC of at least 25 per cent of the working capital gap (total current assets less total current liabilities excluding bank finance). In the second method it brings in NWC of at least 25 per cent of the total current assets. In the third method it brings in, as NWC, 100 per cent of the core current assets and at least 25 per cent of the remaining current assets. The second method results in a current ratio of at least 1.33, the first could result in a lower figure and the third is likely to give a higher one. The working capital limit can then be arrived at by deducting the stipulated NWC and the projected short-term liabilities from the projected total current assets.

Under the cash budget method of assessment the borrower's cash inflows and outflows are projected, usually monthly or quarterly, and bank finance equals the cash deficit, if any. A bank requires working capital finance because on some days the opening cash balance and the cash inflows are not enough for the normal outflows. The statement shows for each period the receipts, the payments (to suppliers, expenses, interest) and the surplus or deficit; the cumulative position, after adding the opening balance, shows the peak cash deficit that the bank finance has to cover.

Under the projected turnover method, known popularly as the Nayak Committee method, it is assumed that the enterprise needs 25 per cent of its annual turnover as gross working capital, of which 20 per cent of turnover is provided by the bank and 5 per cent is brought in as margin by the enterprise. The courseware notes that this may under-finance units whose working capital cycle is longer than three months, so banks also assess the requirement on the holding norms and sanction whichever is higher.
facts.locator: S01 printed p. 453 (the MSE Rs 5 crore rule and digital relaxations on the same page are not taught)

facts.statement: The holding method and the cash budget method both involve projecting the level of activity, credit to customers, credit from suppliers and other current assets and liabilities; the precision of each depends on the credit officer's estimates. The holding method is based on the average of the parameters over the next one year, which may be too long for seasonal industries, so it suits activities with relatively uniform operations and stable markets. The cash budget method suits activities with wide month-to-month fluctuation in the level of activity or market conditions, such as seasonal industries or execution of project contracts. The turnover method suits small enterprises where detailed financial records may not be available.

Bills finance: the borrower submits a statement of book debts and the bank calculates drawing power by deducting the applicable margin. With a bill of exchange drawn by the seller on the purchaser, a demand bill is drawn where no credit is given and is sent with the transport document to the bank for collection or purchase; a usance bill, naming the period of payment and accepted by the purchaser, is drawn where credit is given, and the outstanding is shown as bills receivable. Bills are governed by the Negotiable Instruments Act, which gives more legal protection if the customer defaults. In bills finance the term purchase is normally used for demand bills, discount for usance bills and negotiation for bills drawn under letters of credit opened by the purchaser's bank. A bill purchased, discounted or negotiated is not shown as an asset in the drawer's books; it may appear in her contingent liabilities if the bill is not without recourse to the drawer. At assessment the amount of bills purchased or discounted is added to both current assets and liabilities depending on the bank's loan policy, but negotiated bills are normally not added because the counterparty is another bank and recourse to the drawer is extremely unlikely.

A letter of credit (LC) is an undertaking by the bank, at the request of the buyer (applicant), to pay the seller the contracted amount against compliant documents; its conduct is governed by the ICC publication UCPDC 600. To assess an LC limit the bank estimates the average amount of each LC (from monthly consumption and the economic order quantity), the frequency of opening LCs (12 divided by the number of months of consumption in one LC) and how many LCs will be outstanding at one time, which depends on the lead time, transit time and usance period: the total time an LC remains outstanding divided by the interval between LCs, rounded up. The LC limit is the number outstanding multiplied by the amount of each LC, and because LCs increase credit available to the borrower, the LC limit is normally carved out of the total fund-based working capital limit sanctioned. A bank guarantee limit is likewise carved out of the fund-based need where the guarantee reduces fund-based need (for example a guarantee for receipt of advance payment); a co-acceptance limit is carved out because the credit received from the supplier is not taken into account at assessment.
facts.locator: S01 printed pp. 462-463 (the assessment method only; regulatory guidance on guarantees is in the next batch)

facts.statement: A performance guarantee provides reimbursement to the beneficiary for monetary loss arising from non-performance or under-performance of a contract by the customer (examples: completion of a contract within a time limit, certain quality or satisfactory performance of equipment or a project), while a financial guarantee meets financial obligations or dues of the customer (examples: guarantees in lieu of security deposits, earnest money or payment of dues in case of default). With co-acceptance of bills a supplier is more willing to give credit to the bank's customer because the bill drawn on and accepted by the purchaser is also accepted by the bank, which acts as a guarantee against non-payment by the purchaser.

payload.title: Working capital: gross, net and why a firm needs it
payload.core_explanation_md:
Besides fixed assets, a business holds **current assets**: raw materials, work in process, finished goods and receivables. The money tied up in them is **working capital**.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Gross (total) working capital** | The firm's **total current assets** requirement |
| **Short-term sources** | Credit from **suppliers**, other current liabilities, **bank finance** |
| **Net working capital (NWC)** | The part funded from **long-term sources**: capital or long-term borrowings |

A bank finances the **gap**: it first **assesses the current assets needed**, then expects the enterprise to bring in **some of it from its own capital or long-term money** (the NWC).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is the same NWC as in the financial statements unit: long-term sources less long-term uses, or current assets less current liabilities.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The total requirement of current assets of the enterprise.

payload.title: The operating cycle and why liquidity ratios matter to the banker
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A bank monitors the current ratio each quarter against the sanction condition.

self_check.prompt_text: Which four factors set the length of the operating cycle?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Raw material stock, process time, finished goods stock and credit to purchasers.

payload.title: The holding norms (operating cycle) method
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Step 1 - turnover.** Existing firms: **past performance**. New firms: **production capacity, market share, raw material availability, industry norms**.

**Step 2 - gross working capital** as the sum of:

| Component | What is considered |
| --- | --- |
| **Inventory** | Raw material, work in process, finished goods: **lead time, minimum order quantity, location and number of suppliers, share of imports, process**; industry norms as a guide |
| **Receivables or bills** | **Market practice** for the business |
| **Other current assets** | Cash level, **advances to suppliers**, **advance tax** |

**Step 3 - sources:** **own NWC** (last balance sheet plus internal accruals, with extra NWC if needed for the desired current ratio), **suppliers' credit**, **other current liabilities** (salaries, expenses payable, **customer advances**).

**Bank finance = total working capital - funds from all other sources.**
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The holding method is also called the operating cycle method or the traditional method.

self_check.prompt_text: How is bank finance found under the holding norms method?
self_check.expected_takeaway: As the gap between total working capital and the funds available from all other sources.

payload.title: The three Tandon committee methods of lending
payload.core_explanation_md:
The enterprise is required to bring in NWC as follows (the courseware says some banks still use these):

| Method | NWC the enterprise brings in |
| --- | --- |
| **First** | At least **25 per cent of the working capital gap**, where gap = total current assets - current liabilities **excluding** bank finance |
| **Second** | At least **25 per cent of total current assets** |
| **Third** | **100 per cent of core current assets** plus at least **25 per cent of the remaining** current assets |

**Resulting current ratio:** the **second** method gives **at least 1.33**; the **first** can give **less**; the **third** is likely to give **more**.

**Bank finance** = projected total current assets - stipulated NWC - projected short-term liabilities (other than bank finance).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Core current assets are the permanent minimum level of stocks and similar assets that the firm always holds.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Tandon method gives a current ratio of at least 1.33?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The second method: NWC of at least 25 per cent of total current assets.

payload.title: Bank finance under the three Tandon methods
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm projects total current assets of Rs 400 lakh, of which core current assets are Rs 100 lakh, and current liabilities other than bank finance of Rs 120 lakh. Find the bank finance and the current ratio under each of the three methods.

worked_steps.description: Working capital gap = current assets - other current liabilities.
First method: NWC 25 per cent of the gap; bank finance = gap - NWC.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 210 lakh; current ratio 400 / (120 + 210) = 1.21

worked_steps.description: Second method: NWC 25 per cent of total current assets.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 180 lakh; current ratio 400 / 300 = 1.33

worked_steps.description: Third method: NWC = core (100) + 25 per cent of the remaining 300.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Bank finance Rs 105 lakh; current ratio 400 / 225 = 1.78

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Bank finance: first Rs 210 lakh (current ratio 1.21), second Rs 180 lakh (1.33), third Rs 105 lakh (1.78)

self_check.prompt_text: Which method gives the lowest bank finance and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The third: it asks for the most NWC, since all core current assets are financed from long-term funds.

payload.title: The cash budget method
payload.core_explanation_md:
Project the firm's **cash inflows and outflows** for each month or quarter. **Bank finance = the cash deficit**, if any.

| Period line | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Receipts** | Cash from sales and other inflows |
| **Payments** | Suppliers, expenses, **interest** |
| **Surplus / deficit** | Receipts - payments |
| **Cumulative position** | Opening balance + surplus / deficit, carried forward |

The **lowest cumulative balance** is the **peak deficit** the bank finance must cover.

Why a firm needs bank finance: on some days **opening cash plus inflows** are not enough for **normal outflows**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Monthly projection is more practical than daily projection.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the peak cumulative deficit tell the banker?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The maximum bank finance needed during the period.

payload.title: Peak cash deficit from a three-month cash budget
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm starts January with cash of Rs 20 lakh. Receipts and payments (Rs lakh) are: January 300 and 380; February 280 and 360; March 420 and 350. Find the closing balance each month and the bank finance needed to cover the peak deficit.

worked_steps.description: January net flow, then closing balance.
February net flow, then closing balance.
March net flow, then closing balance.
The peak deficit is the lowest closing balance.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Closing balances -60, -140 and -70; bank finance of Rs 140 lakh covers the peak deficit (end of February)

self_check.prompt_text: Does the bank finance fall to zero at the end of March?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: a deficit of Rs 70 lakh remains, so finance is still needed though less than at the peak.

payload.title: Projected turnover (Nayak) method and choosing a method
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Projected turnover method (Nayak Committee):** the firm needs **25 per cent of annual turnover** as gross working capital: **20 per cent of turnover** from the **bank** and **5 per cent** as **margin** from the firm.

**Weakness:** it can **under-finance** units whose **working capital cycle exceeds three months**, so banks also assess on holding norms and sanction the **higher** amount.

| Method | Best suited to |
| --- | --- |
| **Holding norms** | **Uniform** operations, **stable** markets (it uses a one-year average) |
| **Cash budget** | **Large month-to-month swings**: **seasonal** industries, **project contract** execution |
| **Turnover** | **Small enterprises** without detailed records |

Holding and cash budget methods both project **activity, customer credit, supplier credit and other current items**; both depend on the **credit officer's estimates**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Details of how the turnover method is applied to micro and small enterprises are not taught here because they were not checked against a current instruction.

self_check.prompt_text: Which assessment method suits a seasonal industry?

payload.title: Projected turnover method for a firm with turnover of Rs 200 lakh
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm projects annual turnover of Rs 200 lakh. Find its working capital requirement, the bank finance and the margin under the projected turnover method.

worked_steps.description: Working capital requirement is 25 per cent of turnover.
Bank finance is 20 per cent of turnover.
Margin from the firm is 5 per cent of turnover.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Requirement Rs 50 lakh: bank finance Rs 40 lakh and margin Rs 10 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: What share of the requirement does the bank provide under this method?

payload.title: Bills and receivables finance
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Receivables finance:** the borrower gives a **statement of book debts**; the bank sets **drawing power** by deducting the **margin**.

**Bills of exchange**

| | Demand bill | Usance bill |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When | **No credit** to the buyer | **Credit** for a stated period |
| Accepted by buyer? | Not needed | **Yes**, accepted |
| Shown in seller's books as | **Book debt** (until paid) | **Bills receivable** |
| Bank action | **Collect** or **purchase** | **Discount** after deducting interest for the usance |

Bills are governed by the **Negotiable Instruments Act**, which gives **stronger legal protection** if the buyer defaults.

**Terms:** **purchase** (demand bills), **discount** (usance bills), **negotiation** (bills under an **LC** of the buyer's bank).

**Accounting and assessment:** a bill purchased, discounted or negotiated is **not an asset** of the drawer; it may be a **contingent liability** if it is not **without recourse**. For assessment, bills purchased or discounted are added to **both current assets and current liabilities** as the loan policy says; **negotiated bills are normally not added** (the counterparty is a bank and recourse is very unlikely).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The seller can receive up to 100 per cent of the bill amount on purchase, less usual charges.

self_check.prompt_text: Which kind of bill is normally "discounted"?

payload.title: Letters of credit, guarantees and co-acceptance: how limits are assessed
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Letter of credit (LC):** the bank's undertaking, at the buyer's request, to **pay the seller against compliant documents**; governed by **UCPDC 600** (ICC publication).

**Assessing an LC limit**

1. **Amount of each LC:** from monthly consumption and the **economic order quantity (EOQ)**.
2. **Frequency:** 12 / (months of consumption in one LC).
3. **LCs outstanding at a time:** total time an LC stays outstanding (**lead time + transit + usance**) / interval between LCs, **rounded up**.
4. **LC limit** = LCs outstanding x amount of each LC.

The LC limit is normally **carved out of the fund-based limit**. A **guarantee limit** is carved out where the guarantee reduces fund-based need (for example a guarantee for **receipt of advance payment**), and a **co-acceptance limit** is carved out because **supplier credit** was not counted at assessment.

**Types of guarantee:** a **performance guarantee** protects the beneficiary against **non-performance or under-performance** of a contract; a **financial guarantee** covers **financial obligations or dues** (security deposits, earnest money, payment of dues).

**Co-acceptance:** the bank also **accepts** the bill drawn on its customer, acting as a **guarantee of payment**, so the supplier gives credit more readily.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Regulatory guidance on guarantees and co-acceptances follows in the next batch.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of guarantee covers earnest money?

payload.title: Assessing a letter of credit limit
payload.core_explanation_md: A firm consumes goods worth Rs 9.6 crore a year imported on LC. The EOQ is Rs 1.6 crore. Lead time is 15 days, transit time 15 days and the usance period 3 months. Find the number of LCs a year, the interval between LCs, the time each remains outstanding, the number outstanding at a time and the LC limit.

worked_steps.description: LCs a year = annual consumption / EOQ.
Time each LC stays outstanding: lead + transit + usance.
LCs outstanding at a time = 4 / 2, rounded up.
LC limit = LCs outstanding x amount of each LC.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: 6 LCs a year; one every 2 months; each outstanding 4 months; 2 outstanding at a time; LC limit Rs 3.2 crore (carved out of the fund-based limit)

self_check.prompt_text: If the usance were 5 months, how many LCs would be outstanding at a time?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Time outstanding would be 6 months; 6 / 2 = 3 LCs.
